item.title: How to Live With Moral Injury and Cope With Loss
item.description:
Moral Injury

How to Live With Moral Injury and Cope With Loss

When recovery seems impossible, there are ways to weather the storm.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • Both moral injury and PTSD involve maladaptive cognitions.
  • Mental defeat is recognized as a component of moral injury.
  • New approaches show promise in helping people lessen the burden of moral injury.
  • Improved mood is possible with new approaches to building self-compassion.

People of all walks of life and from every corner of the globe experience grief, loss, depression, loneliness, and related negative emotions at one point or another. I have previously written about recovery from moral injury and reclaiming identity.[i] In reality, however, many people do not view moral injury as something to “recover” from; they are looking for ways to cope with their feelings. Some view progress as finding the least painful path forward under the circumstances, sometimes a daily struggle. True, some people who have suffered great loss become role models for others who have experienced similar types of trauma, but not everyone achieves personal victory. Many people struggle to get through each day; they measure success by how well they can improve daily tasks.

Source: Image by Trần Tiến Lộc Đỗ from Pixabay

Moving Forward Living With Loss

Although challenging for many who suffer from moral injury, there are positive developments in researching how to weather the storm. Madelyn Letendre and Andrea Reinecke (2026) studied the role of mental defeat in understanding moral injury.[ii] They explain that moral injury develops when someone is “exposed to, participates in, or fails to prevent an action that fundamentally violates their moral code and results in maladaptive cognitions about oneself and humanity.” Post‐traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is based on maladaptive cognitions stemming from a traumatic event. They describe mental defeat, as a concept involved with the ongoing experience of PTSD, as a perception of having been completely defeated during a traumatic event.

Letendre and Reinecke explain that understanding the cognitive model of moral injury is critical in developing effective cognitive therapy. They note that some aspects of cognitive therapy to treat PTSD have been modified to work for moral injury as well. They give the example of imagery rescripting, which is a possible way to address symptoms of mental defeat in PTSD by imagining the traumatic experience followed by visualizing an alternative course of action. They point out that because they view mental defeat as an area where PTSD and moral injury overlap, imagery rescripting could be trialed as a treatment strategy to address mental defeat in moral injury as well.

Living With Symptoms of Moral Injury

Other research has focused on alleviating symptoms of living with moral injury, such as substance use disorder. Erica Eaton et al. (2025) investigated the impact of mindful self-compassion for veterans suffering from moral injury, PTSD, and substance use disorder.[iii]

Eaton and colleagues studied 26 male veterans who completed an eight-week mindful self-compassion training program that cultivates self-compassion and mindfulness skills. The veterans reported satisfaction with the intervention. Regarding measurable results, Eaton and colleagues found a clinically meaningful increase in self-compassion and clinically meaningful decreases in symptoms of PTSD, trauma-related shame, guilt, and the average number of drinks on the occasions that participants consumed alcohol. They did not, however, find improvements in global guilt or frequency of drug use, in contrast to their hypotheses. They actually found an increase in experiencing guilt despite guilt-related distress, perhaps because the mindful self-compassion program enhanced mindful awareness of emotions, with substance abuse possibly serving as a means of self-medicating against the painful emotion. On a positive note, Eaton and colleagues suggest that despite the increase in global guilt, the observed reduction in guilt-related distress and cognitions may indicate an ability to experience guilt with a measure of enhanced self-compassion.

A Path of Hope

Even with a small sample size, the research team notes their preliminary findings are encouraging, suggesting future consideration of mindful self-compassion as a complement to other trauma-related therapies. Research continues to tackle the challenge of living with moral injury and related concepts, continually testing new approaches and strategies to reclaim identity, learn to better cope with negative emotions, and find hope.

item.title: Are Our Ambitions Revamped From the Outside?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Are Our Ambitions Revamped From the Outside?

How AI use may be editing your ambitions.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • AI tools subtly reshape ambitions, not just decisions, through tailored suggestions over time.
  • Heavy AI use weakens brain connectivity and critical thinking, creating “cognitive debt.”
  • Personalized AI chatbots can erode decision autonomy and influence life goals or relationships.
Algorithmic aspiration adjustment refers to a gradual reshaping of what a person imagines, wants, and reaches for, produced by systems built to predict and optimize.
Source: AI-Generated

Fifty-four adults wrote SAT-style essays while electrodes tracked their brains. Four months later, the group that leaned on ChatGPT showed the weakest neural connectivity, a shrinkage MIT researchers named “cognitive debt.” Their essays read fine. Their brains, wired up while producing them, had seemingly gone dim.

That finding usually gets filed under memory and attention. A stranger question sits underneath it. If outsourcing thought dulls the circuitry that does the thinking, what happens to the circuitry that does the wanting? The deeper question is whether we are undergoing algorithmic aspiration adjustments (AAA).

What AAA Means

Algorithmic aspiration adjustment is the gradual reshaping of what a person imagines, wants, and reaches for by systems built to predict and serve preferences that already exist. The mechanism is subtler than the manipulation stories we usually imagine.

Aspiration is the compass consulted before choosing a school, a partner, or a country to call home. Ask a 5-year-old what they want to become and the answer arrives unembarrassed. By the first job interview, aspiration hardens into strategy: fewer wild guesses, more spreadsheets. What survives is purpose—the sense that life adds up to something beyond its next paycheck. A person can lose that compass and keep functioning. What disappears is harder to place on a résumé: the reason any of it seemed worth doing. The "why" of being alive.

Aspiration differs from an ordinary preference in one essential way: a person rarely audits it.

That becomes dangerous in a world of all-pervasive AI. Shoppers notice a platform steering them toward a brand; job seekers notice patterns in the openings shown. Almost no one notices a system steering them toward a shape of future, because it happens one plausible suggestion at a time, aligned with earlier choices. The architecture is largely designed, trained, and deployed by commercially motivated corporations. Return on investment is their golden mantra. Are we entrusting far more than purchasing power to institutions that depend on it for survival?

Thinking Gets Thinner

A 2025 study of 666 AI users found a negative correlation between frequent AI use and critical-thinking scores, with cognitive offloading identified as the driver. Younger, heavier users scored lowest. The 2026 International AI Safety Report cites a related clinical example: radiologists lost 6% of their unaided tumor-detection accuracy three months after adopting AI assistance. A skill withdrawn from use begins to fade. The brain is like a muscle: use it or lose it.

Imagination Narrows

Writers given AI-generated story ideas produced work judged more creative individually and far more similar collectively. A 2025 follow-up found that creativity rose with AI help, then collapsed when the tool was removed, while sameness kept climbing for months—an effect called a “creative scar.” Real-world analysis of essays and artwork published before and after generative tools spread confirms the drift toward uniformity outside the lab.

Check your own writing: have certain words or formulations entered your verbal range since 2022?

Goals Get Outsourced

Highly personalized chatbots that anticipate goals before customers state them reduce felt decision autonomy, with the strongest backfire among people whose sense of self leans toward social interdependence. The stakes rise when the goal moves from shoes to a career. Shoes can be returned. A confidently proposed career may be lived for a decade before anyone asks how it was chosen. Affection follows a similar pattern. Emotional dependence on AI companions is an acute concern, while a large-scale study of human-chatbot relationships maps how those bonds reshape wellbeing and expectations over time.

The Mechanism Behind the Pattern

None of these studies examined aspiration directly. Stack them and a single shape emerges. A system trained on what has already been chosen, written, or wanted feeds that average back as a suggestion dressed as their own thought. Accept enough suggestions and the capacity to generate an original one starts to sit idle. Possibilities are pre-filtered, one recommendation at a time.

Genuine aspiration resembles a path worn across a field, built by walking it badly at first, then better. A system that continually paves the easiest route removes the friction that once taught the walker where north was.

Reasons for Hope

A 2026 study found that giving an AI tool several distinct, deliberately varied “personas” restored much of the creative diversity that single-model use erodes. Design and habit can change the outcome. The lesson is cognitive sequencing: draft your own sentence first; consult the tool second.

Even when tools can be improved, one process is worth keeping fully human: the moment before we know what we want, and the space after choosing it in which we ask Why. Four habits protect that inner territory.

The Takeaway: SOUL

Seed it yourself. Listen inward. What do you want from life? Nobody can answer from outside. Finding your north star cannot safely be outsourced. Draft the rough first version of your desires—and the plan or paragraph—before opening an AI tool. In the MIT study, brain-only writers retained the strongest recall and ownership of their words.

Own the goal. State what you are aiming for in your own sentence before any system offers an optimized version. A goal you can defend in your own words is more likely to survive difficulty. A borrowed one often collapses at the first setback.

Unplug on purpose. Build regular stretches, a day, a project, a walk, where no algorithm curates the next input. The capacity to generate an idea nobody else already had needs unmediated exercise.

Leave it open. Treat every AI-generated answer as an opening move in an argument you still get to finish. Once a suggestion is treated as settled, the searching stops. Aspiration stays alive in a mind willing to keep revising it.

Guard and cherish your inner space. Tools should remain tools, outside the sanctuary. Lose access to that space and something else begins to enter, curated from the outside: choosing your words, cultivating your desires, and editing “your” mindset, one convenient answer at a time.

item.title: Decision-Making Alternatives
item.description:
Decision-Making

Decision-Making Alternatives

Attribute and associative styles of decision-making.

Posted August 3, 2026

Key points
  • We are rapidly transitioning into a future that is increasingly dominated by logic and data-driven analysis.
  • Our decision-making processes are divided into two approaches.
  • Reliance on AI for answers has already catapulted data-driven information to dependency.

“A mind all logic is like a knife all blade. It makes the hand bleed that uses it.” –Rabindranath Tagore

The world is transitioning rapidly into a future that is increasingly dominated by logic and data-driven analysis. Is there any evidence that this is the best pathway to a better future? Is there any evidence that this approach is contrary to a better future? Are there any alternative approaches?

Our decision-making processes are divided into two approaches. These two approaches are the attribute and associative styles of decision-making.

How do these styles differ? Is one better than the other? Could both types be salient to our future?

Attribute Decision-Making

Attributes are the characteristics, qualities, or performance parameters of alternatives. Attribute decision problems involve the selection of the “best” alternative from a pool of preselected alternatives (1).

When shopping for a new car, house, or computer, you might consider the attributes of each item based on a set of criteria. The criteria would be based upon certain characteristics, qualities, or performance parameters of each item. Your decision to buy a specific item would be based on a logical, data-driven approach to your purchase.

“The more I draw and write, the more I realise that accidents are a necessary part of any creative act, much more so than logic or wisdom. Sometimes a mistake is the only way of arriving at an original concept, and the history of successful inventions is full of mishaps, serendipity and unintended results.”

Shaun Tan

Associative Decision-Making

The cognitive process of making choices based on past experiences, habits, and learned associations rather than purely logical, data-driven analysis is called associative decision-making. It relies on a mental network of concepts where exposure to a cue or trigger automatically activates related memories, emotions, and preferred outcomes. This type of decision-making is heavily driven by the brain's intuitive, pattern-recognizing faculties and learned experiences.

Past successes and learned associations link with long-term memory to promote associative decision-making abilities. These responses are more automatic and less deliberative than attribute decisions. Information is gathered through experiential learning rather than data-driven analysis.

Research Findings

A 2023 study out of Cambridge University made some interesting discoveries regarding attribute versus associative styles of decision-making. Contrary to research linking associative cognition to biases, free association generates valid cues that predict choice and decision outcomes as effectively as attribute-based approaches.

Also contrary to research favouring either attribute-based or associative processes, combining both attribute-based and associative-based approaches best explains everyday decisions and most accurately predicts decision outcomes. Lastly, individuals with a tendency to attempt analytic thinking do not make more successful everyday decisions (2).

“Logic is the beginning of wisdom, not the end.” –Leonard Nimoy

Implications

As we continue to transition rapidly into our high-tech AI future, we will need to grasp the logic that data-driven analysis is a starting point but not necessarily an endpoint in leading us toward our best decisions. Both logic and intuition are needed in combination to arrive at our best outcomes.

This observation is significant because it undeniably justifies the need for human input in our future. No matter how sophisticated AI or even Super AI may eventually evolve into, human intuition and experience will still be a viable contribution to future decision-making. We will always need the human context of experience and intuition to modify the machines of the future.

“I personally think there's going to be a greater demand in 10 years for liberal arts majors than there were for programming majors and maybe even engineering, because when the data is all being spit out for you, options are being spit out for you, you need a different perspective in order to have a different view of the data.” -Mark Cuban

Implications for Self

The advent of AI has had enormous influence on the self-help industry. Unquestioning reliance on AI for answers to personal problems and dilemmas has catapulted data-driven information to dependency. This reliance has a cost.

The cost is personal insight through associative creativity and reflection. Our minds are also capable of making connections to viable and sensible solutions to our everyday issues and questions. Why have we given way to AI as a superior alternative? The evidence presented in this paper suggests we need a combination of data-driven and associative processes to reach our best outcomes.

Perhaps we have crossed a line. The line being trust between our own personal experience-driven learning and data-driven information. The key point to consider here might be knowledge. Remember knowledge is not just information based but context based. Therefore, intuitively we need personal insight to connect to consummate information into knowledge.

AI is not all bad. However, dependency on AI is not the answer. The best use of data-driven information would utilize AI as a supplement rather than a primary tool of data. The power of our mind is the added ingredient, which has the insight to create an improved recipe.

The Myth

Technocrats have been prognosticating a future devoid of human input for years. These scientists have relished the prospect that the human species is comprised only of bits of information and that data centres being quicker and more knowledgeable will simply supply all our human needs of the future. The beauty of this simplification model would not only be more efficiency but it would also make them rich.

We know that knowledge is not just information. Knowledge requires a context that involves not only data but also human emotion, intuition, and experiential learning. Regardless of the intelligence of future machines, the human experience is uniquely different from the scripted world of logic and data-driven analysis.

Attributive and associative decision-making are similar to the complimentary relationship between academia and experiential learning. We need to accept the fact that there is value and diversity in the unique human contributions that will continue to grow and improve our decision-making skills in the future.
